sources.title: Los Adaes — Cultural Worlds, archival research, and legacy
sources.publisher: Texas Beyond History · Texas Archeological Research Laboratory
sources.author: Hiram F. Gregory, George Avery, Francis X. Galán, Steve Black, and contributors including Mariah F. Wade
sources.annotation: Read Cultural Worlds, Los Adaes Archival Research, Legacy, and the contributor credits. The exhibit distinguishes Adai communities from the colonial establishment and discusses Indigenous-made pottery, trade, and later heritage. Its contributors include an Adai specialist and acknowledge Chief Rufus Davis’s assistance. Some language about disappearance and colonial cultural hierarchies is dated; do not adopt it as a verdict on living identity. The linked exhibit sections count as one resource, not four.

sources.title: The Caddo Indians of Louisiana — second edition, The Adaes section
sources.publisher: Louisiana Division of Archaeology · Anthropological Study No. 2
sources.author: Clarence H. Webb and Hiram F. Gregory
sources.annotation: Inspected the cover, reissue foreword, historical context, and The Adaes section on PDF pp. 22–24. The foreword says this edition largely reissues a 1978 text. A substantial, explicitly Adai-focused account considers dispersed settlement, mission connections, pottery, and possible village identifications. Several sites and affiliations are hypotheses. Its confident Caddoan classification and colonial mission dates require comparison with later specialists; regional archaeological periods do not date the origin of the Adai people. Sensitive locations and funerary details are not reproduced.

sources.title: Presidio Los Adaes: Spanish, French, and Caddoan Interaction on the Northern Frontier
sources.publisher: Historical Archaeology 38(3), pp. 65–77 · Society for Historical Archaeology; authorized Texas Beyond History copy
sources.author: H. F. Gregory, George Avery, Aubra L. Lee, and Jay C. Blaine
sources.annotation: Actual scanned article visually inspected at printed pp. 65, 67–71, and 74–75, including the excavation overview and conclusions. Compares documentary expectations with Indigenous pottery, French and Spanish goods, architecture, and food remains at the presidio. Material patterns concern a mixed colonial settlement; they do not identify every maker as Adai or prove equal power and universal harmony. Site-specific counts and social interpretations need their original contexts. This authored journal study is distinct from the later public exhibit.

proposedParagraphs.title: People, villages, and a colonial place name
proposedParagraphs.text: Los Adaes names a Spanish mission, presidio, and settlement whose history intersects with Adai history. The Texas Beyond History exhibit describes Adai communities maintaining settlements around waterways while visiting and trading with the colonial establishment. Its account also distinguishes the wider region’s peoples and explains why European spellings and administrative categories require scrutiny. A place bearing the Adai name is therefore evidence of a relationship, rather than a complete map of where all Adai families lived. The exhibit’s later heritage discussion acknowledges living communities, even where other passages use older language of disappearance.

proposedParagraphs.title: Archaeological interpretations have their own history
proposedParagraphs.text: Webb and Gregory’s state-published study gives the Adaes a distinct section within its wider Caddo account. It considers dispersed hamlets, trade, pottery, and several possible village identifications. Its wording repeatedly signals uncertainty about particular sites, although it presents some broader classifications more confidently. This is useful evidence of how archaeologists connected documents and material remains at the time. Proposed site identifications and inherited language classifications should remain attributed interpretations, open to comparison with later research and community knowledge.

proposedParagraphs.title: What the presidio’s material remains can show
proposedParagraphs.text: A 2004 journal study compares the colonial record with excavated pottery, imported goods, buildings, and food remains at Los Adaes. Indigenous-made vessels were central to the settlement’s material life, alongside French and Spanish objects. The authors interpret such combinations through exchange and accommodation rather than simply military control. Their evidence concerns a socially mixed settlement: an Indigenous ceramic fragment does not by itself establish an Adai maker, and cooperation in particular activities does not demonstrate equal power in every relationship. The article also treats descendants’ continuing lives as part of the site’s legacy.

unreviewedLeads.title: Documentary Evidence for the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Century Location of the Adaes Indians
unreviewedLeads.author: Darryl Pleasant (repository metadata spells the surname Pleaseant)
unreviewedLeads.scope: Repository abstract inspected; the full article has not yet been obtained. The abstract challenges the assumption that villages clustered immediately around the mission. Do not count the abstract as a completed full-article inspection or draw a boundary from it.
